Analysis of Wood Grain Additives on Crop Growth in Martian Regolith 
 
Maren Beasley, Evan Dang, Sebastian Ezqueda, Kyle Pojol, Kayla Durunna 
Team ID: 23419 
High School Division 
Sprayberry STEM Mars Explorers 
Sprayberry STEM Academy

Abstract 
Our primary focus for the experiment is to test various pinewood forms—sawdust, wood 
chips, and wood shavings—which differ in particle size and water retainment. Based on our 
extensive experience and prior research on the effect Martian Regolith has on plant growth, we 
chose pine wood due to its lightweight properties, affordability, versatility, (Pam, 2024) along 
with the superior moisture retention and dispersion, longevity, and environmental benefits (Snell 
& Snell, 2024). These physical properties within the various wood grain mediums will be 
analyzed to determine influence on plant growth, including factors such as structure, water 
retention, temperature, and nutrient availability. 
Wood grains were mixed throughout the Martian regolith compositions as a water 
transfer medium in varying amounts. To observe the effects that the additive has on amendment 
with plant growth, specifically within Martian regolith. Our previous experiment tested the 
additive of a gel-based nutrient matrix as a nutrient additive. After establishing that our previous 
experiment was successful, we decided to have a new approach to this experiment. 
 For this experiment, our plant choice was chickpeas (Cicer arietinum L.), as it 
demonstrates its adaptability and tolerance to various conditions, specifically in semi-arid and 
arid conditions. With the harsh dry conditions of Mars, the chickpea serves as a promising plant 
to grow, especially when considering the health benefits they provide to the human body. The 
nitrogen fixation properties of chickpeas also serve as a potential outreach in Martian expansion, 
as Mars regolith is void of much nitrogen all together.

Hypothesis 
The addition of pinewood-based amendments will increase porosity and aeration in 
Martian regolith–based mixtures, thereby enhancing water retention and creating more favorable 
conditions for plant growth. We predict that these improvements in structure will lead to higher 
germination rates and healthier overall development of chickpea plants compared to regolith 
without amendments. 
Experimental Design 
In our experiment, we planted Chickpeas into 15 clay pots with various makeup: 7 pots 
containing 100% Earth, 4 pots containing 100% Martian regolith, and 4 pots containing a 50/50 
mix. Three chickpea seeds were planted in each pot to average the data collected. 
Our setup contained 5 groups, Group A with an additive of sawdust, Group B with wood 
shavings, and Group C with wood chips. Group D served as a control group without any 
additives, and Group E served as an Earth timeline for comparison. Groups A, B, and C 
demonstrate the experimental groups for our experiment. The experiment was designed this way 
to ensure the results of the experimental groups were accurate and had control groups to 
accurately contrast the growth without the additives. 
The experiment was conducted in a fume hood, and our team followed a schedule to 
water and monitor growth. The plants receive 40mL of water twice every weekday, once in the 
morning and afternoon. A spaced watering schedule allowed the plants to receive and utilize the 
water over time. Within the fume hood, a 6 hour daily light cycle was installed to keep the data 
consistent.

Variables: 
Independent Variables: 
The experiment manipulated two primary independent variables: composition and 
amendment type. Composition was varied across three levels, pure Martian regolith, pure Earth, 
and a 50/50 Martian–Earth mixture, to assess how differing substrate properties influence plant 
performance.

Each of these types was paired with one of four amendment conditions: sawdust, wood 
shavings, wood chips, no amendment (control), or timeline group. These treatments produced a 
structured matrix of environments that allowed direct evaluation of how composition and organic 
amendment interact to affect plant growth in Martian-regolith systems. 
Dependent Variables: 
Plant growth was quantified by measuring stem height (cm) using a standard metric ruler 
at each observation period. Plant health was assessed through systematic visual inspection of 
morphological traits. Indicators recorded included the presence or absence of leaves, leaf 
coloration (categorized as light green, dark green, or yellowing), and any signs of physiological 
stress or decline (diseased tissue or mold growth). Soil water retention was also measured 
visually to evaluate the effectiveness of moisture retained within the wood additives. These 
metrics served as the primary dependent variables for evaluating plant performance across types 
and treatments. 
Constant: 
Several factors were held constant across all experimental groups to ensure that plant 
responses could be attributed to manipulated conditions rather than external variability. An 
additional Earth-only timeline (group E) functioned as a comparative baseline representing 
optimal terrestrial growing conditions. Mass was standardized, with each pot receiving an equal 
quantity by mass. Seeds were planted with similar depth and spacing. Lighting was controlled by 
an automated timer on a 6-hour interval to ensure a consistent photoperiod. Each pot was sprayed 
ten times every morning with a nutrient-tea solution.

The nutrient tea was prepared by placing fertilizer pellets into distilled water on a hot 
plate stirrer, allowing them to dissolve, then straining the remaining pellet debris, and then 
repeating the process with the leftover material. The concentrated mixture was then diluted to a 
10:1 ratio consisting of 100 mL distilled water and 10 mL of unsaturated nutrient tea. 
Plants were irrigated twice daily with 40 mL of distilled water. Following each irrigation 
event, aeration was performed using a steel rod to reduce surface accumulation and promote 
deeper movement of water and nutrients toward the root zone. By keeping these environmental 
and maintenance conditions constant, the study isolated the effects of composition and 
amendment type as the sole independent variables. 
Results/Discussion and Conclusions 
Through the differing growth occurring within our experiment, substantial data was 
found, deepening our knowledge on the wood grain additive to composition relationship. Within 
our experiment, we found phenomenal growth in experimental groups we did not expect, 
surpassing our standards and expectations. 
Across treatments, plant growth outcomes varied considerably, based on both 
composition and the type of wood-based amendment used. In the Earth-only timeline group 
(Group E), about 80% of the plants germinated and grew successfully, establishing a reliable 
reference point for normal development under favorable terrestrial conditions. As expected, this 
group provided the comparative benchmark for evaluating the effects of Martian regolith 
stimulant and the amendments.

Figure 1: 
 
 
 
 
In the no-additive control (Group D), germination occurred only in the pure Earth and in 
the 50/50 Earth–Martian regolith mixture. No plants germinated in Group D with Martian 
regolith without amendments, reinforcing the well-established limitations of the Martian regolith, 
including poor nutrient availability, low organic content, and inadequate structure for water 
retention and aeration. These results confirm that unmodified Martian regolith cannot 
independently support seed germination under the conditions tested.

The sawdust treatment (Group A) produced the most unexpected and informative 
outcomes. While growth in Earth soil with the sawdust additive occurred for only one seed, 
sawdust was the only amendment that supported germination in all pure Martian regolith. This 
finding is significant because none of the other amendments, nor the control, supported any 
growth in 100% Martian regolith. The fine, structure of sawdust likely enhanced aeration and 
water distribution, allowing for the minimal but successful germination of the chickpea plants. 
Though growth was limited in magnitude, its occurrence demonstrates that sawdust can function 
as an effective amendment for improving the physical qualities of Martian regolith. 
 
 
In contrast, the wood shavings (Group B) and wood chips (Group C) treatments produced more 
limited and comparable results. Each amendment supported germination in one Earth pot and

one 50/50 mixture pot, but neither amendment enabled germination in any pure Martian regolith 
pot. The larger particle size of shavings and chips likely hindered sufficient root contact, reduced 
moisture retention, and provided less uniform aeration compared to the finer sawdust. These 
outcomes highlight that not all wood-based amendments provide the same functional benefits, 
and that particle size plays a critical role in modification.

 Plants also sprouted in the 50/50 mixture. Both the wood shavings (Group B) and wood 
chips (Group C) treatments resulted in limited but comparable outcomes. Each amendment 
supported the germination of one plant in Earth regolith and one plant in the 50/50 Earth-Martian 
regolith mixture, but neither supported any germination in pure Martian regolith. These observed

outcomes reflect the direct effects of the composition and additive type on plant germination and 
survival under the experimental conditions. 
Reflecting on our prior hypothesis; though the wood shavings and wood chip additives 
portrayed similar growth compared to the control and earth-timeline, the amendment of sawdust 
proved the most potential, as growth without any addition Earth was not needed. Due to the size 
of the sawdust grains, both the Martian regolith and sawdust were able to blend exceptionally 
well. The water retention of group A exceeded our initial watering predictions when left 
unattended over a week-long break. Past the growth period, group A was left un-watered, and the 
regolith presented signs of enhanced growth and higher water retention. Unlike the fine particle 
size of the sawdust amendment, we concluded that the wood chips and shavings additive allowed 
for most of the Martian regolith to pass through its larger gaps, leading to the accumulation of 
regolith at the bottom of the pot. Likewise, in the more larger grain compositions like the 50/50 
mix and pure Earth soil, we see how the larger wood grain additives accumulate well with the 
soil and allow for better aeration and water retention compared to the sawdust additives in these 
compositions. 
 
 
Improvements 
Although our experiment had 
growth in most of our groups, there are 
still improvements that can be 
made for future experimentation. A key issue that arose was minimally focusing on the light 
Figure 9

cycle of the plants; we realized that the light was contributing to the plants' deteriorating health. 
Originally the light was kept constant at 12-hour light cycle, 6 hours twice a day, to reduce 
variations in data analysis prior to the experiment. As the experiment progressed, signs of 
yellowing and deterioration were seen among the plants. Through external research about 
chickpea light requirements, we concluded that the light cycle induced among the plants was a 
factor to poor health, reducing the timing to only 6 hours a day, resulting in improved plant 
quality. Henceforth, we plan to adjust the light cycles according to what the individual plants 
need based on data acquired about traditional growth in Earth regolith. 
 In addition to the light cycle, insufficient pot space was an obstacle our team faced. With 
the need to negate error within our experiment, multiple seeds were planted to average data 
among our groups, resulting in the compact conditions of the seeds. Furthermore, a limited 
supply of Martian regolith limited the amount we could add to each pot. Alongside this 
throughout the experiment, the plants became overwatered due to not accounting for how much 
water each additive would retain. To improve future experiments, a greater volume of regolith, a 
shorter light cycle, and a less amount of water would lead to improved growth within our 
experiment.
